title: Nepal Pays for a Climate Crisis It Didn’t Create - Progressive.org
description: Nepal Pays for a Climate Crisis It Didn’t Create  Progressive.org
publisher.title: Progressive.org
full_article:
The wall outside Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, is covered with photographs of people who have not come home.

Relatives look through the rows, stopping at faces they recognize and continuously checking for any new information. For families whose loved ones disappeared in the devastating floods along the Nepal-Tibet border in August, the wall has become a place to wait, search, and hope. Some people were swept away by mountain rivers; others disappeared when floodwaters carrying mud, rocks, and debris tore through villages and hydropower sites.

Because the floods plowed through forests and steep mountain terrain, rescuers have struggled to find missing persons. Routes into some of the worst-hit areas were cut off, turning rescue into a struggle against the landscape itself. The death toll has climbed to more than 1,200, while thousands remain missing.

Nine days after the floods, two workers at a hydropower plant in Nepal’s Rasuwa District became the first survivors to be rescued from a hydropower plant across the affected areas. But weeks later, many other families still do not know whether their loved ones are alive. There is no body to bury, no grave to visit, and no final goodbye. For now, there is only the wall of photographs and the wait for news.

Among those searching is thirty-two-year-old Sarita Ghale, whose five family members remain unaccounted for. “If we cannot find them alive, then at least we want to find their bodies,” Ghale says. “That is our only hope.”

The destruction began with a surge of glacial water that rushed through Nepal’s mountain valleys, leaving communities downstream little time to prepare or evacuate. A landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border caused a flood that travelled sixty-two miles and washed away homes, roads, and bridges.

The United Nations Development Program (UNDP) estimates the floods affected more than 84,000 people across seventeen municipalities and accumulated about 2.2 million tons of debris. The Nepalese government has reported that the country faces $2.56 billion in property, housing, and infrastructure damage.

The disaster unfolded in a Himalaya region that is changing rapidly. Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya, glaciers are losing ice at an accelerating rate: The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development reported in March that the rate of ice loss across the mountain range has doubled since 2000, while glaciers lost about 12 percent of their total area between 1990 and 2020. The region is also seeing more unstable conditions around glaciers, permafrost, and mountain slopes, increasing the potential for cascading hazards such as landslides, debris flows, and glacial lake outburst floods.

Scientists studying the August disaster say climate change should be understood as one factor that may have weakened an already unstable mountain system. A recent assessment by World Weather Attribution found that warming and permafrost degradation likely weakened the rock wall involved in the disaster, while glacier thinning, retreat, and increased meltwater may also have contributed to slope instability. The researchers found that temperatures in July and August near the disaster site were substantially warmer than the historical average, but said they had not assessed whether the specific rock-and-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-caused climate change.

For Nepal, the consequences of these changes are particularly stark. The country contributes only about 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, according to the World Bank, yet its economy and communities are highly exposed to climate-related floods, landslides, water stress, and glacial hazards. In the mountains, hazards can move rapidly from high-altitude slopes into valleys where people live, work, and build infrastructure.

Suriya Bahadur is waiting for rescuers to find his brother, who lived in a nearby village with his wife and child. While Bahadur waits for news, he lives with the agony of uncertainty. For families of the missing, a body is devastating, but it is also an answer. Without it, grief has nowhere to settle.

“I know he may be dead,” he says. “But I cannot believe it until I see his body.”

When the floods began, twenty-eight-year-old Ramesh (who is using a pseudonym for fear of retaliation) was working inside a tunnel under a hydropower plant in the Rasuwa District. Water inundated the tunnel, causing panic among workers, says Anil, who was working with Ramesh in the tunnel and similarly requested a pseudonym. They soon began shouting for help.

“We wanted to go outside, but our supervisor told us to keep working,” Anil says. Soon, their cell signal was disrupted. Outside, families were left calling phones that no longer connected, with no way to know what was happening underground.

A sudden rush of air was followed by a power outage that plunged the tunnel into darkness. One exit was blocked, forcing the workers to search for another way out. “For a moment, we thought we would not make it out,” Ramesh says. Several workers managed to escape through the other side of the tunnel, while others remained trapped.

In the wake of the catastrophic floods, Nepal has to grapple with its development of hydropower as one of its primary economic growth strategies. In the 1990s and 2000s, the Nepalese government increasingly turned its focus to hydropower to address chronic electricity shortages within the country and export electricity to India and Bangladesh—building projects and roads through some of the world’s most geologically fragile terrain. That push has made hydropower central to Nepal’s energy system, while also increasing the country’s exposure to floods and other climate-related hazards in the Himalayas.

Because hydropower plants rely on the flow of water to produce energy, they’re often built in mountains along rivers, making workers vulnerable to seismic and flooding events. There are currently about 900 hydropower plant workers missing beneath the mountains, hundreds of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels, according to army rescuers who spoke to Reuters. At a plant on the Nepal-Tibet border in Rasuwagadhi, authorities are examining reports that dozens of workers may still be alive inside an underground chamber. But rescuers are working through a landscape transformed by the flood: Tunnel entrances are blocked, roads leading to project locations have been washed away, and sections of underground passages are buried under mud and rock.

At least eleven operating hydropower stations and one solar plant were damaged, according to a preliminary UNDP assessment, while fifteen additional hydropower projects under construction were also affected.

The disaster has also raised questions about Nepal’s warning and evacuation systems for hydropower workers and communities downstream in an increasingly unstable mountain environment. The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development reported a rapid rise in water levels in the Bhote Koshi basin on the morning of the August flooding, but it’s unclear whether warnings reached workers inside the tunnels in time to allow them to evacuate.

The Nepalese government has been working to strengthen early-warning systems and incorporate climate risks into infrastructure planning, but there are still major gaps. The World Bank has identified early-warning systems and climate-resilient infrastructure as priorities for Nepal, while the International Center for Integrated Mountain Development has been developing climate-risk assessment guidelines specifically for hydropower projects. Earlier this year, researchers also found limited monitoring of glaciers and other high-altitude hazards, leaving some downstream communities exposed to risks that can be difficult to detect in time.

As glaciers retreat and mountain hazards become harder to predict, uncertainty remains over which entity is responsible for turning information about risks high in the mountains into warnings, evacuation plans, and protections for people living downstream. Nepal’s government agencies, hydropower companies, and local authorities all have roles to play, but the latest flood event exposed the consequences when hazards move faster than systems designed to manage them.

For Sitaram Shah, a survivor in his sixties, the flood did not end when the water receded. It left him facing the harder task of surviving life without his mother and father. He now carries the weight of losing the people he depended on and the financial burden left behind in the wake of the disaster.

“The flood took away the people I depended on and left me with debt, disrupted work and a future I had never planned for,” Shah says.

For survivors like Shah, the flood did not just wash away their homes and possessions—it disrupted the lives built around them, the work that paid the bills, and the families that gave those lives meaning.

And debt does not disappear when a flood does. Families will have to find ways to survive while they search for relatives, repair what they can, and begin again. For Shah and thousands of other survivors, the timeline for recovery will stretch far beyond the rescue operation.

Their rescue did not resolve the fate of those still missing, but it showed families who have spent weeks waiting that the search is not necessarily over. Someone trapped beneath the mountains can still come home.

A building can be rebuilt. A bridge can be replaced. A power station can be repaired. But for those waiting for a missing relative, there is no equivalent measure of loss.

Outside Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, the photographs remain on the wall, and families keep waiting for a phone call, a rescue, or—if hope gives way—a body to bring home.

title: One month after Nepal’s floods, the long road to recovery begins - United Nations Development Programme
description: One month after Nepal’s floods, the long road to recovery begins  United Nations Development Programme
publisher.title: United Nations Development Programme
full_article:
A month ago, water, rock and mud tore through the valleys of northern Nepal with little warning. High in the Himalayas, a huge section of glacier and bedrock had broken away from the north face of Langtang Lirung peak and plunged thousands of feet into the Lhende river below, triggering the deadly cascade. Within minutes, homes were swept away. Roads and bridges vanished beneath floodwater and debris. Families were separated from loved ones. The disaster left thousands of people dead or missing, and communities displaced and cut off from the roads, services and livelihoods they depend on.

The scale of the challenge For those now returning to the worst-affected areas, the destruction is difficult to comprehend, including some 7,570 buildings. “The landscape has completely changed,” says Siddhartha Sharma, National Project Coordinator with UNDP Nepal. “In some places, the river has shifted sideways as much as 100 metres.” Sharma worked on Nepal’s response to the 2015 earthquake. He says the floods have left a different kind of destruction. “The devastation from the floods is much more intense than the earthquake. Nothing is left,” he said. “What used to be a thriving town with schools, markets and homes, now it is just rocks and sand.”

From response to recovery In Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, the emergency response continues. At the same time, another task is becoming urgent: clearing the way forward. Large amounts of mud, sediment and rubble have been deposited. Many roads remain blocked. Farmland has been buried. Buildings and public facilities have been damaged or destroyed. Government assessments estimate around 1 million cubic metres of debris and sediment may need to be cleared. UNDP is supporting National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority-Nepal in using drones and field assessments to map the damage, giving authorities a clearer picture of where debris has accumulated and where access needs to be restored first. The information received from a team of experts from HELP-NGO can help local authorities decide where to clear debris, reopen roads and begin repairs.

title: Climate Justice and Healing for Nepal - Living on Earth

full_article:
Air Date: Week of September 25, 2026

Recovering from a major disaster isn’t just economically challenging, but emotionally traumatic as well, Pandey says. Above, a border crossing between China and Nepal, destroyed by the August 26, 2026 flash flooding. (Photo: CCTV screenshot, Wikimedia Commons, Public Domain)

After the deadly floods in Nepal this August, researchers from the World Weather Attribution group rapidly assessed the event and concluded that climate change played a “very strong” role in the catastrophic glacial collapse. Tanuja Pandey, a climate justice activist and lawyer based in Kathmandu, Nepal, joins Host Paloma Beltran to discuss the human toll of the floods and the moral duty of the world to slow the climate crisis and help Nepal adapt.





Transcript

O’NEILL: It’s Living on Earth, I’m Aynsley O’Neill.

BELTRAN: And I’m Paloma Beltran.

In the weeks following the deadly floods in Nepal this August, researchers from the World Weather Attribution group rapidly assessed the event, and concluded that climate change played a “very strong” role in the catastrophe. Warmer weather melted ice, thawed permafrost, and increased rainfall, destabilizing the glacier before its collapse. Nepal estimates that damages from the floods could exceed $4 billion. That’s over a tenth of the country’s total GDP. For more on this, we turn now to Tanuja Pandey, a climate justice activist and lawyer based in Kathmandu, Nepal. Tanuja originally hails from Sudur Paschim, a region affected by the floods, and she is co-founder and Chair of Harin Nepal, an intersectional climate justice organization. Tanuja, welcome to Living on Earth!

PANDEY: Thank you for having me.

BELTRAN: So it's been nearly a month since devastating floods hit Nepal and Tibet due to glacial collapse in the Himalayas. Talk to us about what you've seen in the weeks since the disaster. You know, how are you and your community holding up?

PANDEY: You know, life after a flood is incredibly difficult, especially for those who have lost someone they love. The water may eventually recede, but the grief does not. And you know, imagine waking up every morning knowing that the person you share your room, your home, your meals, your life is no longer there. And some of the families are still waiting for their loved ones to be found, while others are trying to give a final farewell without having the chance to properly say goodbye. And then they are expected to, you know, rebuild their home, return to their work, and somehow continue with their lives. We often see the images of flood when the water is rising, but we don't see enough of what happens afterward. So it's quite traumatizing to see everything. And when we talk about flood, you know, we talk about the water, the death toll, the missing person. But for communities, the real story, you know, continues long after the water disappears. They are left rebuilding the homes and livelihoods, memories, dignity, and sometimes their entire sense of security. So, it is what Nepal is going through right now, and it's really traumatizing to see everything and to feel helpless because all we can give is sympathy at the moment, even though we want to help with everything we could.



Nepal is a very religious country, Pandey says, and people often associate climate disasters with the actions of spiritual figures. Above, candles lit at Muktinath, an ancient Vishnu temple sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, in Nepal. (Photo: Polyflux, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

BELTRAN: And Tanuja, you visited the affected zones in Nepal. What did you see?

PANDEY: Yeah, you know, I saw the life fading away. I saw the children waiting for their parents. I saw the wife waiting for her husband, a mother waiting for their child, and I saw the entire community, you know, swept away. And the community, it was actually used to be one of the Indigenous land of Nepal, and the community who did nothing to contribute in climate change lost everything within second. And Nepal is one of the very religious country. It's a very sacred country. They worship nature. You know, even today, a lot of climatic disaster is related not to the anthropologic reason, but to the demonic factor in majority part of our country. People don't know what climate change actually is, and I saw people not praying this time, and it was quite heavy for us to see everything, and even heavy for us to talk about it now.

BELTRAN: I'm sure it is. And Nepal estimates that the recovery from the disaster will cost more than $4 billion. Please tell us, you know, what are the non-economic costs that the world should consider regarding this catastrophe that happened in Nepal?

PANDEY: Economic cost is important for everything, but we don't talk about the, you know, amount of anxiety the community had gone through, the amount of fear we have in our mind. You know, a lot of people in mountain communities who lives in downstream are migrating after that event because people are scared to live nearby the water resources, while in fact you know Nepal's historical settlement, traditional settlement has always been nearby the riverside, so it's quite hard to talk about it because we are giving up on our identity, our traditional way of living, just because few countries refuse to stick to their commitment.



Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah has been outspoken about the country’s call for climate justice after the floods. (Photo: Metro News, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0)

BELTRAN: And in the days following the flood, Nepal's government wrote to the United Nations Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, Nepal is requesting $20 million. That's the maximum amount a country can request, and Nepal framed the request in terms of climate justice rather than a request for aid. Tell us about that distinction.

PANDEY: See, the problem is that Nepal's climate story, you know, it often become internationally visible only after a disaster reaches a catastrophic death toll. But in fact, where we lose our people amounting to hundreds, and so on every year, it has become a new normal to us, and that creates a, you know, dangerous cycle. The world responds to the headline event rather than to underlying the accumulating loss and damage, and the factors that is causing the climate crisis at the first hand, and Nepal has done its part. We have restored our forests on an impressive scale, and we are rapidly moving toward clean energy. Even though people don't know what clean energy actually is, and we are promoting the electric mobility and you know implementing the climate adaptation plan at the local level, and we even we are going back to our traditional knowledge, Indigenous practices. Yet a country responsible for less than, you know 0.02% of global greenhouse gas emission is playing an even higher price for a crisis it did not create. Today, our Prime Minister Balendra Shah is leaving to General Assembly. We are not here to blame any nation, but demand what is rightfully ours, and we demand the solidarity and to seek the solution because at this moment we want international communities and polluters' country to stick to it.

BELTRAN: And from what I understand, Nepal has still not received any money from the UN fund. This UN pot of money is severely underfunded because wealthy nations have not contributed what they initially pledged. For example, the United States withdrew from the fund in 2025. What role do wealthier nations have to play in addressing this crisis?



Pandey says wealthier nations have a responsibility to compensate low-emissions countries for climate disasters. Above, supplies from the U.S. Air Force are transported at an airport in Nepal in September 2026. (Photo: United States Air Force, Wikimedia Commons, Public Domain)

PANDEY: So to bounce back from this event like this, you know, we need money. You know, we could have saved our people if we had early warning system. You know, if we had good infrastructure, or if we had invested on preventing everything, so I think financial resources play a huge and most important role when it comes to adaptation. And all these polluters country are making the most out of fossils fuel industry, and all they are doing is they are increasing their wealth, but at the cost of that, country like Nepal are suffering, and it is just against the principle of, basic principle of environmental justice. So, to transitioning away from fossil fuel, it might not be easy for them to do it overnight, but they are in the position to compensate to the communities that are being affected by their actions.

BELTRAN: So, alongside other damages to infrastructure, Nepal estimates that 10% of the country's hydropower capacity was destroyed in the floods. How significant was that energy infrastructure to Nepal?

PANDEY: See, it's not the first time it's happening in Nepal. Even two years ago, we lost our major hydropower plants, and that's why you know we've been saying that no investment is good for Nepal if it is not sustainable or or if it is not green, because you're building hydro plants one day and another day it is being swept away by landslide and flood. So I think we need to re-evaluate all the project, especially the hydropower project we have in Nepal, because a lot of Indigenous community of Nepal actually they were telling the government, and they were asking the government to reevaluate everything because it didn't look sustainable to the community. And the way government sidelined all the Indigenous voices and proceed with the hydropower project, it turned a disaster to Nepal, and we have lost, in fact, we have lost a lot of people inside the hydropower tunnel. Still, thousands are missing. Thousand died inside. So, you know, we of course need development, but it's high time we should start, you know, talking and practicing about sustainable development rather than some colonial practices of development. If we try to build the big skyscraper in Nepal, it will not work here because our soil is not ready for it. We should redefine what development looks like to us, rather than just feeding ourselves the idea of development from the Global North.



Pandey emphasizes that while Nepal needs development, it must do so in a way that is sustainable and community-oriented. Above is Pharping Hydropower Station reservoir, part of Nepal's first historic hydroelectric project. (Photo: Gaurav Dhwaj Khadka, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

BELTRAN: You know, Tanuja, this moment feels like a turning point for many people. The floods in Nepal, the hottest summers on record, and the recent UN report warning about the trajectory of future warming. How, in your view, can we turn this moment into action?

PANDEY: You know, I think for Nepal, even though we have lost thousands of people, thousands are still missing. It's a very sad event. It's a very traumatizing event, but also it's a good opportunity for everyone to get united because what happened today with us could happen to anyone tomorrow. You know, it's not an isolated event. It is not something that will happen for the last time, you know. So we've been seeing the flood everywhere. We've been seeing it in Global South. We've been seeing the heat waves and other stuff in Global North. We need to hear the scientists what they are saying, and we need to actually act with the urgency, rather than you know denying the fact, because the clock is actually ticking and it does not wait for anyone. It didn't wait for Nepal and it will not wait for any other world. It will impact everyone eventually. So I believe that it's a fight of humanity as a whole.

BELTRAN: And Tanuja, what gives you hope?

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Better Chitwan (@betterchitwan)

PANDEY: You know, hope, hope is a very political thing to have, and it is something that does not really help you to survive, but also to thrive. Hope is a very powerful thing to have, and looking at young people confronting their leaders, looking at children trying to educate their parents on what is right and what is wrong in an individual capacity, looking into a grassroot mobilizer working tirelessly, looking at a journalist having a courage to cover issue that is quite hard and challenging for them to do so, and basically looking at humanity to save the humanity itself is something that gives me a hope.

BELTRAN: Tanuja Pandey is a climate justice activist and lawyer based in Nepal. She is a co-founder and chair of Harin Nepal, an intersectional climate justice organization. Tanuja, thanks so much for joining us.

PANDEY: Thank you. Thank you for having me.

title: Climate justice cannot remain a phrase in document: PM Shah - risingnepaldaily.com

publisher.title: risingnepaldaily.com
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter, Kathmandu, Sept. 26: Prime Minister Balendra Shah said at the United Nations General Assembly that those who have contributed more to the problems created by climate change, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Speaking at the Assembly ongoing at New York, on Friday morning, he said, "Climate justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations Document. People of our country be allowed to build their future instead of constantly rebuilding their past."

Stating that Nepal was not at the UN to blame any country or continent, or to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield, he asked one and all to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity.

PM Shah said that climate justice is not only about money but also about distributive justice - who bears the costs, and procedural justice - who has a voice.

It is about whether the future of mountain communities, small island states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and generations yet unborn count equally. "Starting tomorrow at the 'Sagarmatha to the Sea' side-event right here at the United Nations, Nepal is ready to help lead this conversation," he said.

PM Shah has reminded the UNGA that through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international community has already agreed to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

He sought the international solidarity and support in the post-disaster rebuilding. "Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction. After at least 1,400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people still missing, our rapid assessments peg physical recovery needs at about 10 per cent of GDP," he said.

He further added, "We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it. Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becoming unstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable. And every major disaster threatens to erase years of development."

For Nepal – a country that contributed less than 0.1 per cent of the global greenhouse-gas emissions, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency.

"The disaster destroyed roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods. It destroyed clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel our future. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause," said Prime Minister Shah.

According to him, the international system is under now and, many often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard. In such a scenario, Nepal believed it needs a much fairer global economic order. "The weak would not simply have to accept whether the powerful decide," he said.

Referring to the devastating Bhotekoshi floods, termed as 'Himalayan Tsunami', he lamented that he couldn't simply speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation, instead, he was forced speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.

"It was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?" asked the prime minister while recalling the visit of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to Nepal when the latter warned humanity about the madness of an impending climate disaster.

"That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudly enough. We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent to translate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require," he said. "Last month, we saw the tragic consequences."

According to him, this tells us something fundamental - Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.

Stating that the Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet but the part of the planet's life-support system, PM Shah proposed establishing a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China.

He said that this mechanism will help in sharing satellite data and expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes, let us strengthen joint early-warning systems.

He said, "When disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders. Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information."

When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants, maintained the prime minister.

He stressed that Nepal needs adequate grant-based support from the world. The Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate.

"Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help. When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms. We act," he said. "That is what climate justice must mean."

PM meets UN Secretary-General Guterres

Meanwhile, RSS adds: Prime Minister Balendra Shah held a meeting with Secretary-General of the United Nations, Antonio Guterres.

Prime Minister Shah who was in New York in course of attending the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly, had the meeting with the Secretary-General at the UN Headquarters at 6.30 pm local time Thursday evening (4.15 am Friday) before addressing the UNGA, the PM Secretariat informed.

During the meeting, Prime Minister Shah extended gratitude to Secretary-General Guterres for his goodwill toward Nepal and congratulated the latter on his successful tenure.

Highlighting the colossal losses Nepal suffered due to the disaster in the Bhotekoshi River in Rasuwa, Prime Minister Shah noted that the risk of floods from glacial lake outburst remains high.

On the occasion, Secretary-General Guterres expressed deep sympathy for the loss of life and property in the Bhotekoshi disaster and stated that the United Nations stands in solidarity with Nepal on climate issues. The Secretary-General also praised the young Nepali delegation.

Recalling his visit to Nepal as a tourist in 1978, Secretary-General Guterres expressed his commitment to continue supporting Nepal even after his term ends.

Also, there was a discussion between Prime Minister Shah and Secretary-General Guterres about the rehabilitation of riverside residents and green reconstruction.

Matters related to extension of timeline for Nepal's graduation from the Least Developed Countries (LDC) list were also discussed on the occasion, it is stated.

title: Nepal, one month after - nepalitimes.com

publisher.title: nepalitimes.com
full_article:
This Saturday it is exactly one month since the catastrophe on the Bhote Kosi-Trisuli. The death toll in Nepal and China is exceeding 8,000.

One month on, only 110 of the 1,450 recovered bodies have been positively identified and handed over to families.

On Friday morning, Prime Minister Balendra Shah delivered his address to the UN General Assembly where he reminded the world of what befell his nation.

Secretary-General António Guterres mentioned the Nepal disaster in his speech in the context of climate breakdown. But international memory is short, and easily distracted by wars and calamities elsewhere.

The geopolitical climate is not quite right for climate justice. We can raise concerns, but not have unrealistic expectations that rich nations will suddenly develop pangs of guilt about their historical emissions.

It would have been useful for our prime minister after flying all that way to stay longer for the New York Climate Week, and highlight how despite being in the least-developed category, Nepal has done its bit to expand carbon sinks, ensure 100% renewable energy and promote electric transport.

The prime minister is to visit India in November to clear the air with New Delhi. Indian investment in current and future river projects in Nepal will loom large.

Three Indian hydropower projects are being built along the Arun River in a cascade. They are exposed to a domino effect similar to one that hit the Trisuli basin last month that swept away 13 plants. The Arun projects will generate up to 3,000MW in the coming years, nearly 80% of it for export to India.

The Indian parastatal investor must have seen how a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim in October 2023 breached the Chungthang Dam reservoir, sending a debris wave down the Teesta River.

A dam that generated 1,200MW and took six years to build at a cost of $1 billion was destroyed in seconds. Similarly, two major hydropower plants were destroyed in the Chamoli flood in Uttarakhand in 2021.

The Arun River originates in China and has the highest mountain in the world in its catchment. It is fed by glacial lakes that are rapidly expanding. A megaquake in southern Tibet could cause these lakes to burst simultaneously, unleshing a catastrophic flood downstream.

RESETTLE, RELOCATE

Here in Nepal, the most urgent need is to care for the 30,000 people who have lost relatives, homes and livelihoods. Many have now spent a month in shelters. The government has identified locations in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading for survivors.

Families do not just need resettlement, they need safer places, a community and jobs to go back to. People from three villages in Rasuwa that were destroyed in the 2015 earthquake were resettled along the banks of the Trisuli. Many of the 1,400 who survived the earthquake were swept away by last month’s flood.

Nearly 500 children have lost one or both parents, they need counselling, homes and schools. Getting them back to classrooms is the quickest way to restore their routine.

Nearly 14,000 people were rescued through prompt action by the security forces, including from hydropower tunnels which has been the biggest challenge. The Prime Minister’s Relief Fund has received Rs15.06 billion so far, and need-based cash handouts could be the fastest way to get families back on their feet. This is an urgent need, and should not be mired in bureaucracy.

Despite delays and hiccups, the RSP government has been more diligent than previous ones in immediate response. We would have liked to see less grandstanding on social media by some officials, but such stunts come with the territory.

Nepal has not had a break from calamities, political and otherwise, since 1990. We have always bounced back, but that is not the same as having learnt from them. Dasain is a month away, and in characteristic Nepali fashion we could fall back on our legendary apathy and fatalism.

How wisely the RSP government responds to this catastrophe will define its legacy more than anything else.

full_article:
"When the flood left bodies unrecoverable, families in the region asked whether an effigy woven from sacred grass could stand in for the missing dead at the funeral pyre, so that the departed could still be released into their next state," wrote Rajan Khatiwoda in an article in Nepal Times on Friday.

Khatiwoda, an expert in South Asian studies is involved with the Nepal Heritage Documentation Project (NHDP) at the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences, was primarily writing in Nepal Times about how the Rasuwa–Nuwakot flood destroyed shrines, monuments and ghats that stood there for centuries.

advertisement ❮❯

Read Full Story

"We lost neighbours, friends, and collaborators who had opened their homes and memories with us," he wrote describing the local families, priests and caretakers of shrines who helped the NHDP document the intangible heritage of the region.

Saturday is one month of the Rasuwa–Nuwakot flood in Nepal that killed 1,451 people and in which 6,000 are still missing. Of the missing, at least 275 people are from India, according to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). They were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansoravar.

There is no closure for thousands of families of those missing in the mudslide that swept everything in its path away on August 26. Reason tells them that their loved ones are dead, but the heart clutches at hope.

Pramod Poudel has four family members, including his mother and wife, who are missing and tells BBC News he doesn't believe that they will be found.

My heart is still saying that there might be something there, but I have to be realistic and accept that they are not there anymore," Poudel, a 34-year-old who moved from Nepal to East Sussex, in England, in 2009, told the BBC. He said the tragedy struck at a time he was planning to return to Nepal and stay close to his loved ones.

One of the sites where a number of Indians or people of Indian origin were swept away is the Gyirong Port between China and Nepal.

Around 80 people who were on Kailash Mansoravar pilgrimage as part of Sadhguru's Isha Foundation and some team members were at the immigration centre when a wall of water and sludge swept it away.

On August 30, India Today Digital reported that Indians, whose loved ones had gone missing had been contacting embassies, government authorities and rescue teams, and, in some cases, checking recovered bodies, in the hope of finding their relatives.

For some, the wait hasn't ended, even after a month.

MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on September 22 that 275 Indians were missing in the Nepal flash floods of August 26.

An Indian forensic team is working in Kathmandu across several laboratories. The team has been working on around 3,000 samples and has so far generated 1,200 DNA profiles as part of the process to identify remains.

advertisement

With most of the bodies that are pulled out of floodwaters or dug out of mud being damaged beyond recognition, such DNA profiles are practically the only way for relatives to identify their loved ones. Bimala Rokaya, wife of Mohan Lal Rokaya, who is still reported missing, breaks down during his symbolic funeral ceremony at the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu on September 18. (Image: AFP)

THE DISASTER THAT OVERTOOK NEPAL ON AUGUST 26

The stories of people burning effigies to help their loved ones pass on, Indian forensic experts working relentlessly to generate digital profiles, and families still holding on to hope all stem from the disaster that overwhelmed the Himalayan nation last month.

To call the events of August 26 a disaster would be an understatement. It began when an enormous mass of ice and rock detached from the northern flank of the Langtang Lirung peak, at an elevation of around 5,200 metres in Nepal's Himalayas.

advertisement

The ice-rock avalanche transformed into a highly destructive debris flow, sending water, ice, rocks and sediment racing through the Lhende Khola and into the Bhotekoshi river system. The deluge of muddy water swept down from an estimated nearly 2,000 metres (6,560 feet) above sea level.

The torrent tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river valleys, destroying bridges, roads, buildings and hydropower infrastructure along its path.

On the China side of the border, the Gyirong Port was destroyed. In Nepal, Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other downstream districts were severely affected, with settlements inundated or buried under mud and debris and critical infrastructure swept away. The flood eventually travelled through the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli-Narayani system and into downstream areas.

The damage caused was enormous. Thousands of homes, schools, hospitals, roads, bridges were razed into rubble.

A Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment by Nepal’s National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) estimated that rebuilding after the floods would cost $4.73 billion. Of this, $57 million would be needed for immediate relief and short-term reconstruction, while $4.67 billion, or about 10% of Nepal's GDP would be required for long-term reconstruction.

advertisement

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, Nepal's PM Balen Shah called for greater international support for the Herculean reconstruction effort ahead. "When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants," Shah said. "We need adequate grant-based support from the world."

And there is the human cost. As of September 21, Nepal has recovered the bodies of at least 1,451 individuals. An additional 9,287 were injured, while 13,795 people had been rescued so far. Meanwhile, the wherabouts of more than 6,000 souls remain unaccounted for. Rescuers use a wheel loader to rescue a 97-year-old woman following the flash floods. (Image: File)

WHY ARE SO MANY PEOPLE MISSING IN NEPAL?

The unusually high number of people still listed as missing is partly a consequence of the sheer scale and force of the floods. The torrent of water, mud and debris swept people, vehicles and structures into the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river system, carrying bodies hundreds of kilometers downstream.

advertisement

Others may remain buried in mud and debris at destroyed hydropower projects and settlements. Take for instance, the Chilime hydropower project in Rasuwa district, where it took more than a week for teams from the Indian and Nepali Armies to dig through mud-choked tunnels and recover five deceased individuals.

But even when bodies are recovered, identifying them has become another battle. As a September 3 Kathmandu Post report noted, bodies pulled from floodwater can be swollen, discoloured and barely recognisable.

Prolonged soaking can damage skin and fingerprints, while currents strip away clothing and documents. Rocks and debris can fracture bodies or tear limbs from torsos, while mud can conceal tattoos and scars that might otherwise help establish identity.

The longer remains lie in warm, contaminated water, the less useful visual identification becomes, forcing forensic teams to rely on teeth and dense bone, which preserve DNA long after skin and muscle decompose.

At that point, forensic DNA testing may be the only reliable way to establish identity, but the process is painstaking and time-consuming. Of the 1,453 bodies recovered so far, only around 112 have been positively identified and handed over to families. The 19-member Indian forensic team began analysing DNA samples with Nepali counterparts at forensic laboratories in Kathmandu in early September. (Image: X/@IndiaInNepal)

AS HOPE FADES, LOVED ONES TURN TO SYMBOLIC FAREWELLS

Some of the people in Nepal have conducted the funeral of those missing, in an attempt to help with the onward journey of their loved ones.

Twelve-year-old Rozel Shrestha conducted the funeral rites of his father by setting fire to a small effigy of barley and straw, according to an AFP report from earlier this September.

"We searched everywhere, went to morgues across the country, but could not find his body . . . So, the family sat down . . . and decided we have to do our traditional rituals to liberate his soul," AFP quoted Jeevan Shrestha, Rozel's uncle and brother of the deceased, as saying.

It reported that the family of truck driver Chandra Bahadur Newar also conducted his funeral after searching frantically for him for weeks.

"We had to do this to set his soul free, so that he is at peace and happy wherever he is," AFP quoted Newar's wife, Dolma Newar Tamang, as saying.

It has been a full month since floods tore apart Nepal on August 26. Reconstruction is ongoing. Debris are being trucked away. Bulldozers and wheel loaders are roaring away as roads are cleared and bridges are erected. The Prime Minister, Balen Shah, is warning the world about the dangers of climate change and garnering international support to rebuild his nation.

The world is beginning to move on from the catastrophe. But for the loved ones of the more than 6,000 people still reduced to names on a missing persons list, closure may remain difficult, if not impossible, to find.

- Ends

CHENNAI: A month after the tragic Nepal flash floods that left hundreds from across the world missing, 85 pilgrims from Tamil Nadu remain untraceable. For their families, grappling with agony has become part of everyday life. They met NRT Welfare Minister K Thennarasu on September 15 and even held a hunger strike at Singaperumal Koil on September 21, seeking updates. With no concrete information on the whereabouts of their loved ones, they say they have been left to fight the battle largely on their own. Some said they are ready to travel to Nepal and assist in rescue operations.

Talking to TNIE about the tragedy losing visibility in the media, N Maravel (55) of Chromepet, owner of Mahadev Kailash Yatra that took 49 pilgrims to Nepal who are still missing, said, “Maybe we have become old news. There are so many things happening across Tamil Nadu and Chennai every day that nobody wants to talk about our issue anymore.”

Maravel’s son N Sathya Narayanan (28), who led the 48 pilgrims from Chennai, is also missing. The group had completed their visit to the Himalayas and were inside a Chinese immigration facility when the floods hit.

“I’m a spiritual man, and we, as a family, are believers in astrology. We were told that Sathya Narayanan is alive in a place where he is unable to contact us. He is stuck in a place where there is a language issue. We are hopeful. His nine-month-old son is awaiting his return,” Maravel said.

title: Address by the Rt. Hon. Prime Minister Mr Balendra Shah to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York - Ministry of Foreign Affairs Nepal
description: Address by the Rt. Hon. Prime Minister Mr Balendra Shah to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York  Ministry of Foreign Affairs Nepal
publisher.title: Ministry of Foreign Affairs Nepal
full_article:
81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly

Remarks by the Rt. Hon. Balendra Shah, Prime Minister of Nepal

September 24, 2026

New York

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

I come before you from Nepal - a distant country in the Himalayas - carrying a close warning for humanity.

I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.

Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.

About families waiting for loved ones who will never come home.

About communities searching through mud, rocks and water for people whose bodies may never be recovered.

About bridges, roads, schools, homes and livelihoods swept away in minutes.

And about a country whose steady progress to achieve Sustainable Development Goals has been interrupted.

====

Four weeks ago, the world saw the shocking images of the catastrophic flash floods that swept through Nepal’s mountain communities with ferocity many have called a “Himalayan Tsunami.”

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.

And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?

Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the Secretary-General of the United Nations warned humanity about the madness of an impending climate disaster.

That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudly enough.

We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it.

Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence.

But we, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent to translate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require.

Last month, we saw the tragic consequences.

=====

A warming climate is destabilizing the fragile Himalayan ecology.

Melting permafrost are fracturing mountain slopes beneath the glaciers and accelerating the risks of ice-rock avalanche, floods, landslides and other cascading hazards.

The resulting devastation unleashed havoc on both sides of the Nepal-China border. The flood continued downstream towards India.

This tells us something fundamental:

Climate change does not recognize borders.

Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.

Excellencies,

I am not here to complain but to share some suggestions.

First, I wish to express Nepal's deep gratitude to all those who came to our aid in the aftermath of the deluge.

Our immediate neighbors, India and China, offered prompt and generous assistance.

Other friendly countries, the United Nations system, humanitarian agencies, philanthropies and people around the world stood with Nepal.

To all of them, I say: thank you on behalf of the grateful people of Nepal.

Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction.

After at least 1400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people still missing, our rapid assessments peg physical recovery needs at about 10 percent of GDP.

As in rebuilding after past disasters like the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, we count on your solidarity and support.

But we must also understand why this disaster matters beyond Nepal.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions.

We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it.

Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becoming unstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable.

And every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.

For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency.

It destroys roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods.

It destroys clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel our future.

And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause.

=====

But we are not here to blame any country or continent.

We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield.

We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity.

Through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international community has already agreed to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

Those who have historically contributed more to the problem, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations Document.

People of our country be allowed to build their future instead of constantly rebuilding their past.

========

Excellencies,

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly two billion people. These mountains provide water, ecosystems, agriculture and livelihoods to populations far beyond Nepal.

The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system.

That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that we establish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China.

Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise.

Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes.

Let us strengthen joint early-warning systems.

And when disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders.

Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information.

Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playing a global role exceeding its ecological share.

We have restored forests to cover nearly half our territory.

We are installing hydro power at a pace enough to power all our clean energy needs and displace dirty sources abroad.

We are promoting electric mobility with an adoption rate to match parts of Europe.

We are strengthening climate adaptation at the local level. And we shall do more to withstand increased intensity and frequency of climate disasters.

=====

But, Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis made worse by the failure of global governance.

That is why this Assembly must note six words:

Relief. Rehabilitation. Reconstruction.

And also:

Responsibility. Reparation. Resilience.

The first three are what we need after disaster.

The second three are what we need to ensure that disaster does not become a permanent condition.

When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants.

We need adequate grant-based support from the world. The Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate.

Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help.

When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms.

We act.

That is what climate justice must mean.

========

Excellencies,

This brings me to a larger question:

What kind of international order do we want?

The United Nations was born from humanity's experience of horrific World Wars.

Its promise was that sovereignty would matter.

International law would matter.

The dignity of every human being would matter.

And the weak would not simply have to accept whatever the powerful decide.

Today, that international system is under strain.

Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard.

Nepal believes we need a much fairer global economic order.

========

In 1994, UNDP’s Human Development Report conceptualized the notion of human insecurity.

It equated security with people rather than territories, and with development rather than arms. It called for the peace dividend to secure f reedoms from fear and want.

The new majority government in Nepal, elected through the fairest and most peaceful elections in our history this March, has had to weather many international adversities since.

When a poor farmer in Nepal went to sow her seeds this monsoon, fertilizers didn’t reach her on time. When we wanted to pave a new highway, there was no bitumen. When a family sat down for an evening meal, there was shortage of cooking fuel.

On the one hand, there are melting glaciers and failing harvests to floods arriving without warning. On the other, a global supply chain punishes poor people for causes beyond reason.

Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline. But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.

We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food.

And this is not Nepal's private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask Sri Lanka. Ask any other country in our region and you will hear the same account: hit by the climate we did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start.

This tells us there is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of global cooperation.

Excellencies,

I am told I am the youngest Head of Government to address this Assembly this year.

I did not come here to make that the story.

I came to make sure that whatever else is said from this podium, one thing is said plainly: a country that is willing to pay should be able to buy, and a world that can deliver a weapon anywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without means for a decent livelihood.

This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism. This is why we need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt, and we can work together towards just outcomes.

Climate justice is, therefore, not only about money.

It is about distributive justice - who bears the costs.

It is about procedural justice - who has a voice.

It is about whether the future of mountain communities, small island states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and generations yet unborn count equally.

Starting tomorrow at the “Sagarmatha to the Sea” side-event right here at the United Nations, Nepal is ready to help lead this conversation.

======

Mr. President & Excellencies,

We are at this General Assembly at a moment of profound global uncertainty — and with a renewed democratic mandate that reflects the aspirations of a new generation.

Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability.

This generational shift is not only a national story. It is part of a global awakening against conflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.

The commitment of my government is clear: to build a state that delivers — decent jobs, social protection, and a fair chance for every Nepali to thrive at home.

The Nepal floods signal a future shaped by rising climate extremes. Our baselines are no longer relevant. And we must move from ad-hoc responses to a culture of preparedness.

Let us finance resilience, and invest in insurance and innovation.

Let us build stronger infrastructure and institutions.

Let us reduce fossil-fuel dependence.

Let us build systems that warn, alert and save lives.

Let us reform the order that leaves the weakest with the least power.

And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world:

Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.

भगवान पशुपतिनाथले विश्वको कल्याण गरुन्।

यो विश्व बुद्धले देखाएको बाटोमा हिंड्न सकोस्।

title: From the Himalayas to the islands, Nepal calls for a united climate response - The Kathmandu Post
description: From the Himalayas to the islands, Nepal calls for a united climate response  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal brought together an unusual coalition of mountain and island nations at the United Nations on Saturday, seeking to turn the country’s recent climate disaster into a broader push for international cooperation stretching from the Himalayas to some of the world’s lowest-lying countries.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal convened representatives from Bhutan, the Maldives, New Zealand, Samoa, Tajikistan and other countries alongside senior UN officials for a high-level meeting titled “Sagarmatha to the Sea: A Call to Action for a Climate-Resilient Future,” held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The Nepal-led gathering was built around a simple premise that borders may divide countries, but water does not.

“The climate system does not recognise the boundaries through which we organise our politics,” said Khanal.

At one end is Sagarmatha, or Mount Everest. At the other are island nations such as the Maldives and Samoa, where rising seas and coastal erosion are already threatening communities.

Through the event Nepal sought to bring the two into the same conversation, arguing that melting glaciers, changing river systems and rising seas are not separate crises, but different consequences of the same warming planet.

“The mountain and the sea may appear far apart on the map, but nature tells us otherwise,” Khanal said. “The water that leaves our glaciers continues its journey, so do the consequences of the choices we make today.”

The meeting came exactly one month after a massive collapse of rock and glacier ice along the Nepal-China border on August 26 triggered devastating flooding, killing hundreds of people and destroying homes and critical infrastructure.

“The wounds are still fresh,” he added. “There could hardly be a more timely moment for this conversation.”

The disaster loomed over much of the discussion, with one speaker after another offering condolences to Nepal and China before returning to a common question: whether vulnerable countries have the resources to see the next disaster coming.

Ambassador Tenzin Rondel Wongchuk, a representative from Bhutan, pointed to two glacier disasters to illustrate the stakes.

In May 2025, a glacier and rock mass collapsed above the Swiss village of Blatten, largely destroying it. But scientists had been monitoring the mountain for years, and when sensors detected signs of an imminent collapse, authorities evacuated residents days in advance. Livestock were flown out by helicopter, including cows, nearly 200 sheep and even rabbits. Only one person was killed.

Then, this year, a similar disaster unfolded in the Himalayas just a month ago.

“Two glaciers failed. Two valleys flooded with rocks and ice,” Wongchuk said. “In one, cows, sheep and rabbits were saved. In the other, thousands of people were not.”

For Bhutan’s representative, the contrast came down to access to the tools that can turn an approaching disaster into an early warning.

“This is a story about asymmetry in the tools nations have to see danger coming,” he said. “The physics of a warming planet does not discriminate, but our capacity to predict, to warn and to respond remains sharply and unfairly divided along lines of wealth and geography.”

That disparity, and the effort to close it, emerged as a central theme of the meeting Nepal convened.

Khanal called for stronger early-warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, scientific cooperation and greater access to climate finance and technology for developing countries. He also urged greater international attention to mountain regions in global climate negotiations and called for the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage to be adequately financed and accessible to vulnerable countries.

“Climate justice is tangible when responsibility, capacity and vulnerability are reflected in the support countries receive,” he said.

Nepal has lost close to a third of its ice in recent decades, according to Khanal. The wider Himalayan region contains more than 63,000 glaciers and represents the largest concentration of snow and ice outside the polar regions.

However, those glaciers are not only a Nepali concern. Mountains provide between 55 and 60 percent of the world’s annual freshwater flowers, the president of the UN General Assembly Khalilur Rahman told the gathering, while around two billion people depend on mountain water for their lives and livelihoods.

In 2024, glaciers worldwide lost approximately 450 billion tonnes of ice—enough to raise global sea levels by around 1.2 millimetres in a single year, he said. All monitored glaciers in High Mountain Asia lost mass in 2025.

“Climate change respects no borders, and its impacts do not remain confined to the places where they begin,” he said.

The connection allowed Nepal to find common ground with countries whose geography could hardly look more different.

“What happens in the mountains does not stay there; its consequences travel downstream, across borders, and ultimately to our coasts,” said Iruthisham Adam, Maldives foreign minister.

For the Maldives, that means rising seas, coastal erosion and increasing pressure on island communities. For Samoa, it means saltwater entering freshwater supplies, changing ocean conditions and growing threats to infrastructure and livelihoods.

Tajikistan brought another mountain perspective. Around 1,300 of the country’s glaciers have disappeared over the past 50 years, a representative of the country said. Globally, the world’s 19 assessed glacier regions lost more than 6,500 gigatonnes of ice between 2000 and 2023.

The gathering allowed Nepal to turn attention on the Himalayas into a call for cooperation among climate-vulnerable countries that face different threats but share demands for better forecasting, technology and access to climate finance.

New Zealand, itself both mountainous and surrounded by ocean, praised Nepal for bringing those constituencies together.

A riverside community buried in mud and debris after severe flooding along the Bhotekoshi river. Post photo

“Nepal has shown important leadership in bringing attention to the connections between climate impacts in mountain regions and those experienced far beyond them,” its representative Ministry of Foreign Affairs Deputy Secretary Gabrielle Rush said.

New Zealand also announced that it had contributed $3.5 million toward humanitarian organisations supporting Nepal’s response to the August disaster.

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage has separately received a request for support from Nepal, one of its representatives told the meeting. The fund remains in a pilot phase, but its board is considering Nepal’s request.

Norway has provided 10 million Norwegian kroner in humanitarian assistance following the floods, including support for shelter, clean water and health services.

China, which was also affected by the August cross-border disaster, said it had dispatched rescue experts and shared satellite imagery and hydrological data with Nepal.

“China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers,” its representative said.

But several speakers argued that international assistance after disasters was not enough, and that countries needed the tangible ability to act before catastrophe arrived.

A UNDP official pointed to advances in satellite imagery, artificial intelligence and climate modelling that can help identify danger earlier. “The real test is whether we can use this before disaster strikes, not after,” she said.

UN Environment Programme officials similarly argued that investment in monitoring, early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure could substantially reduce future losses.

The Hindu Kush Himalayan region feeds 10 major river systems that support the lives and livelihoods of as many as two billion people, a UNEP representative said. Changes to a glacier or watershed can therefore travel hundreds or thousands of kilometres downstream.

The UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific and Nepal will convene another regional meeting in Bangkok next month to advance cooperation on early-warning systems, data sharing and coordinated climate adaptation, officials announced Friday.

For Nepal, the New York gathering also marked an attempt to keep mountain countries more firmly on the international climate agenda. The country convened the first Sagarmatha Sambaas in 2025 around climate change, mountains and the future of humanity, and Khanal said Nepal plans to host a second edition next year. He presented “Sagarmatha to the Sea” as another platform through which Nepal hopes to build cooperation among governments, scientists, financial institutions and vulnerable communities.

Khanal also highlighted Nepal’s own climate efforts, noting that forests cover around 46 percent of the country and that hydropower and electric mobility are expanding.

But Nepal used the meeting to make a larger case that the forces reshaping the Himalayas do not stay there.

Mountain nations spoke of retreating glaciers, while island nations warned of shrinking coastlines. Others pointed to the rivers that connect the mountains to the sea.

Through out the discussion, speakers returned to the August disaster in Nepal as an example of the future at stake.
